 Open enrollment brings robocalls, scams targeting health care plan seekers 
 Scammers may pose as government officials, Medicare representatives or insurance providers 
 Open enrollment is underway, and the period for choosing health care plans for the year ahead is also a popular time for scammers and robocalls. By Matt Venezia Published : Nov. 10, 2026 at 6:18 AM CST | Updated : 3 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google BATON ROUGE, La. (WAFB) - Open enrollment is underway, and the period for choosing health care plans for the year ahead is also a popular time for scammers and robocalls.
 Organizations like the Better Business Bureau receive many robocall and scam complaints around this time of year. The general open enrollment window opened Nov. 1. The Medicare open enrollment window opened a few weeks earlier, on October 15.
 Who scammers target
 Scammers may pose as government officials, Medicare representatives or insurance providers. They tend to go after beneficiaries, senior citizens and people eligible for Medicare.
 A robocall or an email can appear real and convincing.
 Five warning signs of a Medicare scam
 The National Council on Aging lists five warning signs of a Medicare scam:
 Someone promises free items or services. 
 Someone pressures you to switch your Medicare plan. 
 Someone threatens to cancel your coverage. 
 A message says you are eligible for a refund. 
 A claim says you need to renew or upgrade your Medicare card. 
 Carmen Million, president of the South Louisiana chapter of the Better Business Bureau, said people should ask for documentation.
 “If somebody tells you that you have a certain amount of coverage, get that in writing,” Million said.
 How scammers reach consumers
 The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services estimates Medicare fraud, waste and abuse cost taxpayers and the health care system roughly $60 billion to more than $100 billion annually. 
 During open enrollment, scammers often reach consumers through websites that appear accurate and safe. Misspellings in graphics or hyperlinks can be a sign of a scam.
 Phone calls and links in text messages are other ways scammers try to gain access to personal information, such as Medicare numbers, Social Security numbers, insurance details or banking data.
 Artificial intelligence has also made it easier to be fooled by these scams.
 “AI is involved in this. AI can make any commercial, any ad, any text and any call seem valid,” Million said.
 Federal health care fraud charges
 Earlier this year, the Justice Department announced a national health care fraud takedown . It led to 455 defendants being charged in alleged participation in health care fraud and opioid abuse.
 The schemes involved more than $6.5 billion in false claims and significant patient harm.
 Reporting scams
 People who come across scams can report them using the Better Business Bureau’s Scam Tracker.
